speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: asked the Minister for Education in respect of the recent cybersecurity incident involving the Mobile Guardian Device Management Application which has affected students in Singapore (a) what is the Ministry doing to help students who have had their study notes wiped out; (b) whether the Ministry has reviewed such software installed in tablets used by students to ensure that similar incidents do not recur; and (c) what necessary action will the Ministry take against the supplier of the software.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: asked the Minister for Education with regard to the recent cybersecurity incident involving the Mobile Guardian Device Management Application that has affected students in Singapore (a) whether an update can be provided on how the Ministry is helping students who have been affected; and (b) what steps are being taken to ensure that similar incidents do not occur again in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: asked the Minister for Education whether there will be a review of the usage of technology by our students after the global cyber-security breach of the Mobile Guardian Device Management Application that affected our secondary students.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: asked the Minister for Education whether there will be a review done of our students' usage of technology for learning to assess if there has been an over-reliance on technology to the detriment of our students, including losing learning notes that the students have recorded and kept on their school-issued devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) on what date did the Ministry first become aware of security vulnerabilities in the Mobile Guardian system; (b) what immediate steps were taken within the first 24 hours upon discovery; and (c) whether the vulnerability was immediately verified and patched, bearing in mind its critical nature and ease of exploitation and, if not, why not.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) how are schools managing the devices of students after the Mobile Guardian Device Management Application was removed from their devices following the security breach in August 2024; (b) whether the Ministry has plans to involve parents more in the management of their children's devices; and (c) what specific steps will the Ministry take to empower parents with the knowledge and tools to effectively manage their children's devices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) how many students are unable to recover data from their devices following the Mobile Guardian cybersecurity incident in August 2024; (b) how will the Ministry assist these students; and (c) how will the Ministry manage mobile device security to prevent future incidents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In addition, I will also address two Written PQs by Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Gerald Giam, and I invite Members to seek clarifications, as needed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The DMA supports students, as they learn, to use their personal learning devices (PLDs) safely and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, DMA blocks students' access to undesirable Internet content, such as gambling or pornography, and sets screen time limits.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will now share what happened in April and the actions taken by the Ministry of Education (MOE).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The incident in April was due to poor password management practice within Mobile Guardian, allowing the attacker to gain unauthorised access to Mobile Guardians' Management Portal, which led to the data breach.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To ensure continued safe use, Mobile Guardian immediately locked down its admin accounts and mandated all account holders to change their passwords.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I had told this House in May, Mobile Guardians' Management Portal is used for administrative purposes and does not have the ability to change any configuration on students' PLDs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Mobile Guardian app was, thus, not affected during the April incident.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOE immediately registered strong dissatisfaction to Mobile Guardian over the incident and asked that an independent forensic investigator be appointed to evaluate Mobile Guardian systems and processes, and make recommendations to prevent a recurrence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Subsequent findings from the forensic investigator pointed to poor password management practices and Mobile Guardian responded by implementing additional security measures, such as strengthening authentication controls and fixing vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the night of 30 May, a member of the public reported a potential vulnerability in the Mobile Guardian app to MOE.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our information technology (IT) security team immediately investigated the report in the morning of 31 May.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, as explained earlier, because Mobile Guardian had rolled out a patch just before, attempts to replicate the vulnerability disclosed by the member of public was not successful.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: An independent certified penetration tester engaged by Mobile Guardian to conduct additional penetration tests in June further confirmed that this vulnerability reported by the member of the public, had been closed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The independent test uncovered new vulnerabilities, which Mobile Guardian had committed to fix.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, before it could complete the work, some schools started reporting, on 30 July, that some PLDs had lost the ability to connect to the Internet and, in some cases, total loss of usage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We quickly established then that this glitch was not related to the April data breach incident, neither was it a cyberattack.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, it was due to a human error by a Mobile Guardian engineer, who configured a wrong expiry date, causing the app to stop working.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To rectify the misconfiguration, an online update to the Mobile Guardian application was immediately deployed to all iPad users.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To contain the breach, Mobile Guardian immediately shut down their servers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a precautionary measure, MOE embarked on the systematic removal of the Mobile Guardian app from all iPad and Chromebook PLDs the next day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our priority was to help affected students, particularly those sitting for national examinations, so that learning and revision could continue.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We deployed over 300 additional IT engineers and staff to schools to help students restore their devices as well as provided instruction sheets to those students who wanted to troubleshoot their own devices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All devices have since been restored for use last month.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: During this period, schools made available hard copy learning resources while supporting students who were emotionally affected.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Deadlines for assignments were extended and weighted assessments postponed, where needed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students can continue to access learning resources on the Singapore Student Learning Space, or SLS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through this episode, it was most heartening to see many of our students step forward and proactively share their personal notes with classmates and organise study sessions to do revision for their tests and examinations together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We thank the vigilant members of the public who had flagged the potential vulnerability, our colleagues in the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) and the Cybersecurity Agency (CSA), and also the media community, who rallied around MOE to give the much-needed support, which helped our students learn the positives during this incident.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOE requires our IT service providers to keep our systems and data safe.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our forensic investigations with GovTech and CSA into the 4 August incident, found a new vulnerability in the Mobile Guardian system that could allow an individual to carry out the attack.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is a timely reminder that cyber threats can evolve quickly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While no security test can be entirely exhaustive, MOE expects its contractors to regularly assess and strengthen their system's security posture.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While the recent spate of incidents was highly unfortunate, this must not deter us from delivering education through technology as they enrich our students' learning experiences.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must learn to embrace educational technology in our teaching and learning so that our students grow up to be digitally savvy, able to navigate digital environments and take on the opportunities and challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All of us can learn from this incident.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is an important reminder for all of us to practise good digital hygiene, including the regular backing up of information.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With the experience that we have gained, a DMA has been very helpful in helping us to deter people from entering unsavoury sites, maybe intentionally or unintentionally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Every year, every month, not an insignificant amount of sites or attempts at entry to such sites were blocked.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, there is a need for the cybersecurity, the cyber hygiene and the cyber wellness of our students that they have such a DMA.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, I would also want to say that a DMA also provides a range of options that MOE can work with parents on their desired and appropriate level of controls.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The other 25%, or one quarter of them, are split between some who wanted stricter controls; and some who want less strict controls.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are able to cater to the different needs of the parents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I can declare that there are Clementi students who are affected by this and a number could not recover some of their lost data.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister two supplementary questions on behalf of these Clementi students and their parents?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask if the forensic investigation contractor was nominated by Mobile Guardian or nominated by MOE?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Did MOE have any say in the choice of the contractor to do the audit for the May 2024 data breach incident?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister if MOE is working with CSA and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) to ensure that the same standards of cybersecurity for Government networks that face the public, these same standards are also being applied to contractors such as Mobile Guardian or whatever replaces it in the future, so that the attack surface for cyber threats is contained and has the same level of safety, regardless of whether it is a contractor or whether it is Government's own device management technology?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So that we can see the results of both and that is why I have explained in my answer that we have found new vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want to explain that every time we do regular penetration tests, we will have to regularly update the app.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not possible to say you do a test one time and you will be safe forever.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Threats are emerging every day, every other moment and we have to just make sure we regularly do our checks to make sure that things are okay.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second question, I would rephrase what Dr Tan had said slightly differently.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When you say same level of safety and security for all systems, I think that is not the right basis for us to work on.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The attack surface is wide in the cyber security domain.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not possible for us to defend everywhere with the same resources, with the same level of focus.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the military, there is a saying that if you defend everywhere, you defend nowhere.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In any system, whether big or small, personal or national, government or non-government, we will have to prioritise our resources to see where are the most critical areas that we need to defend against and invest more resources in.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, in our national framework – in a separate PQ answer, I think MDDI will share this – is that at the highest level, we have what we call the Critical Information Infrastructure, the CII.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the type of systems we will devote the most resources to, to make sure that they are the most robust.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then, there are cascading, different levels of security required.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is a risk-based approach that we adopt.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In managing our cybersecurity, from the highest CII level to the other levels, there will be different resources required, there will be different areas of focus required.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We cannot be adopting the same defence posture for all the different systems.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I just hope that we have a shared understanding in this House on this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, while there might be differing levels of security and resources devoted to different systems, whenever there is an incident, it is in the collective interest of all of us to learn from it to see how the system might have been compromised or penetrated.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why when something like that happens, we require any contractor to do their own independent forensic investigation, let us know the results.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also do our own independent forensic to see whether the results match or whether there are blind spots that each of us may not have been able to detect prior to that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would not use the phrase that we have the same level of security and safety for all systems because I do not think that will be practical and I do not think that is the end goal of what we are trying to achieve.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because the Mobile Guardian has full control over the devices, including to remote wipe the device, it is more akin to a corporate managed device which should be regularly backed up by MOE in case of a malicious data attack.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Was this a full VAPT and were all the vulnerabilities discovered patched before the August cyber attack?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And was there a VAPT conducted on Mobile Guardian before it was first rolled out?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For any software as a system, before we acquire the system — and by the way, I think nowadays, all of us use software as a service, SAAS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, in all our mobile devices or otherwise, we have such things there.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Before we acquire a service, we do various tests and we make sure that the various systems are also up to the international standards.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is what we do, before we subscribe to any service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Similar to Mobile Guardian, similar to other services, we look at the price quality matrices to see which service meets our needs and is at a price that is reasonable for our needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What we can say is that the issues that were found in June, July onwards, were progressively being fixed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On his first supplementary question, I think it is an important lesson that in an era where we are all dependent on technology, to regularly back up our own systems.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would say that even before technology comes about, even once upon a time when we take notes with pen and paper, I think we also did the necessary back-up because it is just a good habit for us to do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, we also know just as how we manage our own personal devices and Government devices, there are two levels of back-up.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Every one of us have to do our own individual back-up on certain parts of the notes that we want and there are also system level back-ups on the system level issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it will not be possible for the system to back up the individual one, all the time, because the individual, you need to decide what you want to back up.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am quite sure all of us will store some things in our smartphones.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The numbers, I have stated in my answer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a major issue and had major consequences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister, are we over reliant on iPads and IT to the prejudice of our students and conventional teaching?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Point number two, so much is now being deflected to screen time for learning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Point number three, I have been told that even some primary schools issue iPads to Primary 4 students.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth supplementary question, I have studied this – over reliance on screen learning dulls the mind.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The abacus or the calculator in the mind becomes slow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even Minister Chan talks about doing mathematics in Cantonese in his mind.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No amount of parental guidance can stop gaming and possibly even pornography.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I wish to put on record these concerns as supplementary questions and before doing so, I declare that I am a parent of four children who are involved in iPad learning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is my own view that too much learning is done on the screen, but as a matter of being a Member of Parliament, I will also state that the schools in the ward that I am responsible for, were affected by this shutdown and affected quite badly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Chan, if you can keep your answer short because I am trying to squeeze in a few more supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, no, I think it is not about whether we are over-reliant or not over-reliant.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will have to learn to use technology, couple that with the best pedagogical practices, and that balance will continue to evolve as our society evolves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, yes, we are concerned with screen time but we are also concerned with the type of screen time and the ages at which people are exposed to screen time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have explained in this House before, that at different ages we are concerned with different types of screen time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For the very, very young, if they are watching a YouTube movie unsupervised, that has probably the greatest damage and is our greatest concern.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When they are a bit older, it might be games.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And when they are even older, it might be social media.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it depends on what they use the screen time for.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If they use the screen time for educational purposes and are supervised, and have constant interactions with adults, I think the effect is quite different from what we have described just now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But having said that, we do allow our primary schools to use electronic devices for education purposes and they share the resources around.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it is not a personal learning device; it is a group learning device and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We had a few schools that have embarked on a trial to see the more intensive use of learning devices in schools with the supervision of the teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are at the preliminary stage of looking at the experiences of these few schools.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is why, going forward, we will have to see what type of screen time for what purpose, what amount and what age.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will MOE take a look at the impact of this episode on students, especially those who had all the data wiped out, and the outcome of their examinations?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will their examination results be moderated according to this incident?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The answer is yes, but I want to put in context the scale of the issue.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think I have shared how many students are involved – it is not as if all the students lost everything.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The students actually do have access to various resources and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, at the local school level, where it is not national examinations, we have made the local adjustments according to the school's circumstances and needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think my school leaders have done that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When we contract for software as a service, we all know that there will be certain risks involved when we subscribe to any of these software as a service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the selection process, I think one of the things in any agencies, government or commercial, that we must be conscious of is that we can make a choice between two extremes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One is subscribe to a service that is generally available but not customised.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It may not meet your needs but it may be more accessible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The other one is that you can try to make it much more customised according to your needs but you require a unique solution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Somewhere between these two, you must find that balance because both sides have risks, whether you use a widely accessible software as a service solution, which has its pluses and minuses – you can change and evolve much faster because the subscriber base is much bigger, but you may not have all the services you require.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you go for customised service, you might not have all the services and the updates as quickly as you want because it is much more customised, according to your needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, somewhere between these two, we must always find the balance, according to the different risk profiles and the different needs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now read the Orders of the day.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
